transcript: The document object model is a programming interface for web documents. It allows JavaScript to dynamically manipulate content structure and styling. So when you open a web page, your browser doesn't just display the raw HTML. It reads, analyzes, and structures it in a way that makes sense for rendering and interaction. This process is called parsing where the browser scans through the HTML code, identifies different elements like headings, paragraph, images, and links and then builds a structured representation of the entire document known as a DOM or document object model. Think of it like assembling a puzzle. The browser takes the individual pieces, in this case HTML tags, understands their relationships, and organizes them into a treelike structure where each node represents an element on the page.

title: 🤖 MCP Will Change How You Think About AI Integration
transcript: Imagine you have a very smart friend, an AI, who can talk about many topics. But this friend doesn't know how to use your phone apps or browse the web for upto-date information. Modular component protocol or MCP is like giving that smart friend a universal tool belt or a set of plugins so they can use other tools and access information outside their own mind. In simple terms, MCP is an open set of rules, a protocol that lets AI programs, especially those powered by LLMs, connect and interact with external tools, data, and services. Think of it as a universal adapter that lets AI assistants integrate with cloud apps, databases, file systems, and more. In this video, we are diving deep into what MCP is and why it's important. how MCP enables AI to use external tools, a technical breakdown of how MCP works, and how engineers can integrate MCP into their systems. By the end of this video, you'll fully understand MCP and see how it can unlock new capabilities in AI applications. So, let's get started. [Music] Normally, an AI model is limited to what's in its training data or what the user provides in a prompt. With MCP, the AI can ask for help from external helpers. For example, fetching today's weather from an API, searching a document, or executing a calculation, all through a standardized procedure. This means the AI isn't stuck in isolation. It can reach out and use tools just like you would. MCP defines a common language for the AI, the LLM, and tools to talk. An AI that understands MCP can request to use a tool via this protocol. And the tool wrapped in an MCP server will do the action and return the result. It's as if the AI says, I need to check something in the database. And MCP is the agreed upon way to ask and get an answer. The magic is that the AI doesn't need to know the technical details of the database or web service. MCP handles that communication in the background. Consider an AI writing assistant. Without MCP, if you wanted to include information from your calendar or files, you would have to copy paste that info yourself. With MCP, the assistant on its own retrieve your schedule from Google calendar or search your Google Drive via an MCP integration and incorporate that info into its answers. In fact, there are already example MCP connectors for services like Google Drive and Slack, allowing an AI agent to search your files or send messages for you. In everyday terms, MCP brings several simple benefits to AI applications. It has got easier connections, so no need for complex coding each time you want an AI to use a new tool. MCP provides a standard way to plug tools, so it just works. It's modular, so you can add remove tools. Think of them as attachments or apps for AI without breaking everything. The AI can adapt to new tasks by gaining new MCP modules, much like adding apps to your phone. And because the AI can fetch relevant data or use a precise tool when needed, it can give more accurate and up-to-date answers. For example, it could look up the latest news or perform math rather than guessing. And if a tool or data source changes, you update that component, the MCP server, without retraining the AI or rewriting the whole AI application. This is like updating one plug-in instead of redesigning the entire system. MCP encourages secure handling of data in actions. So you or developers can set what the AI is allowed to do. For instance, an AI might have access to calculator but not to your personal emails unless you permit it. MCP was introduced by Anthropic in late 2024 as an open standard for connecting AI models with external data and tools. It follows a client server model similar to how a web browser communicates with a website. In MCP's world, we have host application or the AI agent. This is the main AI powered system like a chatbot, coding assistant or a voice assistant. Now, the terms AI agent and AI assistant are often used interchangeably. But there is a subtle difference. AI assistant is a broad term referring to any AI system that helps user perform tasks. For example, chat GPT, Google Assistant, Microsoft Copilot, or Replate Cohostriter. AI agent is a more specific term used in AI development, referring to an autonomous system that can make decisions, interact with external tools, and complete tasks without direct human input. So a basic AI assistant just answers questions while an AI agent can take autonomous actions like fetching data, modifying files or executing code. In MCP architecture, an AI agent is a type of AI assistant that actively interacts with external tools to achieve goals. It includes the LLMs or the large language model and decision-making logic that determines when to call external tools. The MCP client is a component inside the AI agent or our AI assistant. It acts as a connector or driver between the AI and external tools which is MCP service in this case. The AI agent does not communicate with tools directly. Instead, it relies on the MCP client to handle the interaction. For instance, if our AI agent wants to connect to both a calendar and a database, it would spawn two MCP clients, one for each server. MCP server is the external tool or data source wrapped in the MCP interface. It's a programmer service that offers capabilities, context, actions, data to the AI via the protocol. The server could be local that is running on the same machine or remote a cloud service and can provide things like files from your desk, results from a web API or operations or tools like sending an email. A local MCP server is an MCP server that only serves request from MCP clients running on the same machine. It does not talk to external services or accept request from outside devices. A remote MCP server means it is accessible remotely. It can run on your local machine or external machine. For example, you're running an MCP server on your local machine or cloud that interacts with Google Drive, GitHub or Postgress SQL. MCP server interacts with these external services by running MCP tools. MCP tools are the external functions, APIs or actions that an AI assistant can use via MCP. So the MCP client sends a request like this and the MCP server runs the tool, retrieves the file from Google Drive and sends the result back. The AI assistant then uses the result in its response. And there are several types of MCV tools you can find. Search tool fetches realtime data from the web. The email tool sends emails on behalf of the user. Calendar tool checks availability and schedules meetings. Database query tool can retrieve structured data from a database. And a file access tool reads or write files from a secure location. Now on the AI assistant side, the MCP client may handle internal capabilities like secure file access and sampling. These allow the AI to interact securely with local data or manage how it requests external assistance. The server provides three types of capabilities to the AI. Prompts, resources, tools, and functions. Prompts are predefined instructions or templates that help guide the AI on how to interact with the tool efficiently. Think of them as AI friendly hints for better responses. Resources are like external data sources the AI can query such as databases, APIs or file systems. Tools and functions are actions the AI can perform like sending emails, running calculations or executing commands. So when your AI assistant needs a real world information or actions, it uses MCP to send a request via the MCP client. The transport layer delivers it to the MCP server and the server processes it using prompts, resources or tools before sending the response back. The transport layer is what allows the MCP client and MCP server to communicate just like how the internet allows websites and apps to exchange data. MCP messages follow the JSON RPC 2.0 protocol which is structured way for computers to send and receive requests remotely. But JSON RPC itself is transport agnostic meaning it does not dictate how messages are sent and that's where the transport layer comes in. It ensures that JSON RPC messages travel between the client and server reliably. MCP can use different transport methods such as standard input output or stdio for local communication between processes or server send events or SSE for real-time updates over the web. It can also use websockets, HTTP or even custom transport layers for cloud-based AI agents. And like I said earlier, MCP uses JSON RPC 2.0 as the communication format. This means the client and server exchange messages in a structured JSON format including request responses and notifications. The protocol is transport agnostic, but the current common methods are stdio for local connections and SSE for remote connections. In practice, a local MCP server might just read or write JSON messages via the console to talk to the AI host, whereas a remote one could maintain a persistent SSH channel over HTTP. The MCP schema defines a set of messages types and structures, for example, how a tool invocation request looks or how a resource query response is formatted, etc. The good news is that there are already SDKs to handle this for you. For example, the official Python SDK and TypeScript SDK provide highle classes to create MCP clients and servers without dealing with raw JSON serialization for every message. Here is a highle view of implementing MCP. Suppose you want to expose a new data source or capability via MCP. You would implement an MTP server using the Python SDK. For instance, you might subclass or use decorators to define tools and resources. For example, using this pseudo code. In this simplified example, I have defined a tool and a resource. The SDK would handle packaging the function names, arguments, etc. into the MCP protocol format. Running the server would open a JSON RPC channel over stddio IO here. Waiting for the AI client to call send email or request get latest report. Real implementation will also include registering those capability descriptors so the client knows what's available. For engineers, think of this like defining RPC methods that the client can invoke remotely. Now, as far as running the MCP server is concerned, you can deploy MCB servers in various ways. Locally, it could just be a background process or a thread. Remotely, it might be a microser. So for local deployments like integrating with a desktop app or local agent running via stddio IO is convenient. You might launch the server process and pipe its input or output. For remote you typically wrap the servers run loop to use an HTTP or SSE connection. And in fact some SDKs might help with this. On the AI or host side you will instantiate an MCP client and connect it to the server. And with the Python SDK this could be as simple as this code. Now in a real world scenario when integrating MCP with an AI model you need a loop that manages when and how the model calls external tools and this is often called as the LLM loop. The LLM loop is a process that takes the AI model's output that is what it wants to do and then decides if a tool is needed. For example, if the AI says let me check your calendar it should call a calendar tool. It then invokes the right MCP tool. For example, calling client.invoke tool with tool name and parameters and then feeds the result back to the AI model so it can use the tools response in its reply. title: what is jwt authentication?
transcript: JWT which stands for Json web token is a compact stateless mechanism for API authentication when a user logs into an application the API server creates a digitally signed and encrypted JWT that includes the user's identity the client then includes the JWT in every subsequent request which the server deserializes and validates the users data is therefore not stored on the server side which improves scalability JWT authentication is popular because it allows the server to issue tokens that clients can use to authenticate themselves in future request the token contains information about the user and is signed meaning it can't be tampered with it's stateless so the server doesn't need to store session data JWT authentication has become a go-to solution for securing apis in scalable stateless environments if you want to dive deeper into how jwt's work check out my previous video where I explain how Json web tokens ensure both security and efficiency

websites and online application deliver their content quickly to users all over the world even if they are located far away from the website server for example if a user is in New York wants to access responsive even during periods of high traffic let's go through a simplified explanation of how CDN works when a user types A www.youtube.com into the browser so here we have a user who types
